title: Wide-bandgap charge well that never needs refresh
idea: IFR: a bit that holds itself forever with zero leakage. Closest achievable: store the bit as a deep-depletion charge well in a 4H-SiC (3.3 eV) MOS capacitor with a SiC access FET, where thermal generation scales as exp(-Eg/2kT) and falls by roughly 10^16x vs silicon, so retention moves from ms to hours.
why: Fact 3 (leakage tail/refresh): refresh energy and its 16-33% idle-power and 10-20% bandwidth tax go to near zero; with retention no longer limiting, Cs can shrink, easing fact 1.

title: Non-contact bistable buckled nanobeam as a mechanical bit
idea: IFR: a bit held by geometry that costs nothing to keep. Closest achievable: a ~50 nm compressively prestressed SiC or graphene beam buckles up or down (two energy minima), is flipped by a ns electrostatic pulse from side electrodes and read capacitively; it never touches anything, so there is no stiction or wear.
why: Zero retention energy and no refresh (fact 3), no capacitor charge wall (fact 1); GHz-class beams switch in ~1-10 ns; endurance effectively unlimited because there is no contact.

title: Air-gap NEMS relay replaces the leaky access transistor
idea: IFR: an access switch whose off-state is perfect emptiness. Closest achievable: a vertical nanoelectromechanical relay (TiN cantilever, ~5 nm air gap) gates each storage capacitor; off-state leakage is tunnelling through air (<1e-21 A), so today's 5 fF capacitor holds charge for minutes to hours.
why: Fact 3: removes the <=13 fA tail and refresh power; with retention solved, Cs can fall 5-10x and break the aspect-ratio wall (fact 1). Contact endurance is the main risk.

title: Sliding-ferroelectric bilayer stacking registry as the bit
idea: IFR: switch the bit by nudging atoms, not by pushing charge across barriers. Closest achievable: in rhombohedral bilayer hBN or MoS2 the AB vs BA stacking registry carries opposite out-of-plane polarization; a ~0.3 V pulse slides one layer by one bond length and the polarization is read as a threshold shift in an adjacent 2D channel.
why: Facts 1 and 10: no capacitor, sub-volt write (CV^2 down ~10x), atomically thin so tiers stack for 3D (fact 2); sliding has a tiny barrier and reported fatigue-free switching.

title: Polar skyrmion topological charge as an unforgettable bit
idea: IFR: a bit that thermal noise cannot flip because it is topologically protected. Closest achievable: in PbTiO3/SrTiO3 superlattices, nucleate or annihilate a ~10 nm polar skyrmion with a local electrode field and read its presence through its distinct local permittivity or piezoresponse.
why: Density (~10 nm bits, below 4F^2) and retention without refresh (fact 3); no ion motion so endurance is effectively unlimited; sidesteps capacitor scaling (fact 1).

title: Antiferromagnetic Mn3Sn bit flipped by spin-orbit torque
idea: IFR: a bit with no stray field, no wear and picosecond speed. Closest achievable: a noncollinear antiferromagnet (Mn3Sn) whose magnetic octupole order is switched by spin-orbit torque from a heavy-metal line and read via its large anomalous Hall or tunnelling signal; zero stray field lets cells pack at minimum pitch.
why: Nonvolatile and wear-free, so no refresh (fact 3) and immune to charge-coupled row hammer (fact 9); density gain from zero dipolar crosstalk.

title: Superionic nanolayer pseudocapacitor packs 30x charge per pillar
idea: IFR: a capacitor with infinite charge density that charges instantly. Closest achievable: line the pillar with a ~3 nm superionic conductor (alpha-AgI or Cu2Se class, ionic diffusivity ~1e-5 cm^2/s) between blocking electrodes so ions cross the film in ~25 ns, storing pseudocapacitive charge 10-30x that of a dielectric of equal area.
why: Fact 1: delivers the Cs that AR 115 or k 70 would, at AR ~10-20; fewer deep-etch steps lower capital (fact 4).

title: Negative-capacitance superlattice dielectric hitting effective k of 100
idea: IFR: a dielectric with infinite permittivity. Closest achievable: stack 1 nm ferroelectric HZO with 1 nm Al2O3 in a superlattice tuned so the dielectric stabilizes the ferroelectric's negative-capacitance branch, multiplying net capacitance 2-4x without hysteresis.
why: Fact 1: reaches the k~70 target with existing ALD materials, letting AR fall from ~115 back to ~40.

title: Twenty-electron Coulomb island read by an in-cell single-electron sensor
idea: IFR: storing a bit needs only a few electrons. Closest achievable: hold ~20 electrons on a 3 nm silicon island whose Coulomb charging energy (>kT) blocks leakage, sensed nondestructively by an adjacent single-electron transistor whose current shifts a full period per electron.
why: Fact 1 disappears (required charge falls ~1000x) and so does fact 8 (destructive read); write energy drops to the aJ scale.

title: Conductive ferroelectric domain wall bit read by current
idea: IFR: read the bit without disturbing it. Closest achievable: in a thin LiNbO3 or BiFeO3 mesa a write pulse creates or erases a charged domain wall between two side electrodes; reading passes a small current only when the conductive wall exists, leaving polarization untouched.
why: Fact 8: nondestructive read removes restore energy and permits small fetch granules; nonvolatile so no refresh; domains switch in sub-ns.

title: Acoustic recirculating delay-line memory: bits stored as phonons in flight
idea: IFR: memory with no cells at all. Closest achievable: store bit streams as GHz acoustic pulses circulating in thin-film LiNbO3 or AlN on-chip delay loops (sound is 10^5x slower than light, so 1 mm holds ~1000 bits at 4 GHz), regenerated each lap by a small amplifier; many short loops keep average latency near 100 ns.
why: Capital intensity (fact 4): needs no capacitors and no fine lithography, only piezo films; fits streaming KV-cache and weight traffic that is accessed sequentially.

title: Bistable photonic-crystal nanocavity holding a bit as trapped light
idea: IFR: a bit that moves at light speed with no resistive loss. Closest achievable: an InP or Si photonic-crystal nanocavity with Kerr or carrier bistability holds high or low intracavity intensity under a shared bias beam (~tens of nW hold), written by fJ pulses and read on a waveguide bus.
why: Fact 5: data-movement energy falls because the bit already lives on the optical interconnect; ps switching.

title: Hysteretic Mott latch: niobium dioxide cell held inside its loop
idea: IFR: a cell that latches itself with no transistor and no capacitor. Closest achievable: bias a nanoscale NbO2 device through a series resistor at a hold voltage inside its insulator-metal hysteresis window so either phase is stable; a short over- or under-voltage pulse flips it and reading senses the ~10^3 resistance ratio.
why: Facts 1 and 7: a one-element 4F^2 volatile latch with no capacitor, ns switching and no filament wear-out.

title: Esaki tunnel-diode pair that self-refreshes the storage node
idea: IFR: a charge bit that pulls itself back when it leaks. Closest achievable: hang two series interband tunnel diodes (Si/SiGe or oxide heterojunction) on the storage node so their negative differential resistance creates two stable node voltages fed by a pA standby current, turning the 1T1C into a static cell.
why: Fact 3: refresh (46 fJ/bit, bandwidth loss) eliminated while keeping near-1T1C area.

title: Proton-position gate: bit stored as hydrogen location in gate
idea: IFR: store a bit by moving the lightest ion a few nanometres. Closest achievable: a gain cell whose read-transistor gate holds a ~5 nm proton conductor (phosphosilicate glass or hydrated HfO2) capped by an H-blocking layer; ns pulses shuttle protons toward or away from the channel, shifting threshold, and read is nondestructive.
why: Facts 1 and 8: no capacitor and nondestructive read; protons have been moved at ns timescales in nm films, giving seconds of retention with low-voltage writes.

title: Charge-density-wave hidden state in tantalum disulfide as bit
idea: IFR: a bit stored in the electron crystal itself. Closest achievable: in thin 1T-TaS2 a ps-to-ns voltage pulse switches the commensurate charge-density wave into a metastable mosaic metallic state and a longer pulse restores it; read is the ~10x resistance change.
why: fJ-scale switching with no capacitor (fact 1) and no ion migration, so endurance is high; needs the hidden state stabilized at room temperature.

title: Dealloyed nanoporous electrode multiplies capacitor area tenfold
idea: IFR: infinite capacitor area in zero footprint. Closest achievable: deposit a binary alloy liner (e.g. Ag-Au or Al-Ti) in the pillar, selectively dissolve one metal to leave a nanoporous sponge electrode with ~5 nm ligaments, then ALD-coat dielectric and top electrode for 5-10x surface area.
why: Fact 1: 5 fF at AR ~20 instead of 60-75; shorter deep etches cut tool time and capital (fact 4).

title: Asymmetric ferroelectric capacitor read by small-signal capacitance
idea: IFR: read polarization without ever flipping it. Closest achievable: build a ferroelectric capacitor with dissimilar electrodes (e.g. TiN vs WOx) so up and down polarization produce different depletion and thus different small-signal capacitance; a tiny AC probe below the coercive field reads the bit.
why: Fact 8: removes destructive read and its ~5.9 pJ/useful-bit restore, and relieves ferroelectric endurance limits because reads never switch.

title: NEMS parametron: bit as the phase of a vibrating beam
idea: IFR: a bit made of motion, free to keep if lossless. Closest achievable: a high-Q nanomechanical resonator pumped at twice its frequency oscillates in one of two degenerate phases (0 or pi); a small seed signal sets the phase (write) and phase-sensitive detection reads it, reviving Goto's 1950s parametron.
why: Facts 3 and 9: no charge to leak or hammer; one shared pump replaces per-cell refresh; near-reversible dynamics allow sub-fJ writes.

title: n-i-p-i doping superlattice storing separated electrons and holes
idea: IFR: charge that can never recombine. Closest achievable: a Dohler n-i-p-i superlattice (alternating n and p doping sheets) separates electrons and holes into different layers, stretching recombination lifetimes toward seconds; many periods stack charge vertically in one cell footprint.
why: Facts 1 and 3: stored charge scales with period count (epitaxial, no high-AR etch) and retention is long.

title: Nested triple-coaxial cylinder capacitor like an MLCC in a pillar
idea: IFR: every bit of cell volume is capacitor plate. Closest achievable: build three concentric electrodes inside one pillar hole by alternating ALD electrode, dielectric and sacrificial layers, tying alternate shells together at top and bottom as an MLCC interdigitates its plates.
why: Fact 1: ~2.5-3x Cs per pillar vs a single cylinder, so AR can fall from ~70 to ~30.

title: Vortex nanoring core memory threaded by word and bit lines
idea: IFR: core memory's unlimited endurance at nanoscale. Closest achievable: permalloy nanorings threaded by a vertical via hold clockwise or counter-clockwise vortex chirality, set by coincident current in the via and a bitline as in 1950s cores, and read by a small TMR stack on the ring.
why: Nonvolatile, unlimited endurance, closed flux means no stray field (row-hammer immune, fact 9) and no capacitor (fact 1).

title: Storage-element prize judged on a common 300 mm test vehicle
idea: IFR: the perfect bit shows up because everyone tries. Closest achievable: a $50M tiered prize (<=4F^2, >=1 s retention, <=10 ns, >=1e15 cycles) where finalists integrate their storage element on a shared U.S. 300 mm wafer that already carries real sense amps and periphery.
why: Speeds storage-element discovery and U.S. manufacturability; the shared periphery wafer cuts each team's capital need ~100x.

title: Printed ferroelectric nematic liquid crystal bit that heals itself
idea: IFR: a ferroelectric that cannot fatigue because it is liquid. Closest achievable: inkjet ferroelectric nematic mesogens (RM734/DIO class, P ~6 uC/cm^2) into printed microwells between printed electrodes; polarization is read capacitively and the fluid order regrows after every switch (us today, targeting ~100 ns in nanowells).
why: Endurance with ferroelectric-class charge, fully printable at low temperature; R2R cost per bit.

title: Roll-to-roll anodized aluminium foil gives 150:1 capacitor pores free
idea: IFR: high-aspect holes that etch themselves. Closest achievable: anodize aluminium foil on a reel so self-ordered alumina pores grow ~20 nm wide and ~3 um deep (AR ~150) with no lithography, then spatial-ALD TiN/ZrO2/TiN inside to form capacitor arrays laminated onto access-device layers.
why: Facts 1 and 4: passes AR 115 with zero EUV and zero plasma etch, on abundant aluminium.

title: Printed redox-molecule monolayer storing quantized charge per molecule
idea: IFR: every molecule is an identical, perfect capacitor. Closest achievable: print a self-assembled monolayer of porphyrin or ferrocene molecules on printed electrodes; each molecule holds 1-2 electrons at sharp redox potentials, giving ~10 uC/cm^2 and natural multilevel states with seconds-to-minutes retention.
why: Fact 1: areal charge 10-100x an oxide capacitor, solution-printable; multilevel raises bits per cell.

title: Printed ionogel double-layer capacitor shrinking the charge wall
idea: IFR: a dielectric one molecule thick. Closest achievable: print an ion gel (ionic liquid in polymer) between blocking electrodes; the electric double layer acts as a ~1 nm dielectric giving ~10 uF/cm^2 (hundreds of times a 5 nm high-k film), with nano-thin gels pushing charging toward sub-us.
why: Fact 1: 5 fF fits a planar ~0.05 um^2 pad with no high-AR etch; R2R printable.

title: Printed proton-transfer organic ferroelectric with low coercive voltage
idea: IFR: polarization that flips without moving heavy atoms. Closest achievable: solution-print croconic acid or diisopropylammonium bromide films whose polarization reverses by proton hopping along hydrogen bonds (P ~20 uC/cm^2) at low field, used as printed capacitors in a 2T nondestructive-read gain configuration.
why: Fact 10 and capital: organic ferroelectric printed below 150 C with remanent polarization comparable to HZO.

title: Liquid-metal droplet position bit in printed microchannels
idea: IFR: a bit held by surface tension at zero power. Closest achievable: a sub-um gallium-alloy droplet rests in one of two pinned pockets of a printed channel; an electrocapillary pulse moves it and the bit is read as the capacitance of the occupied pocket.
why: Unlimited endurance (no solid wear), zero retention power, printable; latency scales with size and is the main risk.

title: Printed alpha-indium-selenide ferroelectric semiconductor flake ink
idea: IFR: a channel that remembers by itself with no separate dielectric. Closest achievable: inkjet exfoliated alpha-In2Se3 nanoflakes, a 2D ferroelectric semiconductor whose locked in-plane/out-of-plane polarization modulates its own conductance, so each printed flake is a two-terminal or FET bit.
why: No capacitor (fact 1), low-temperature printing, sub-volt switching; no oxygen-vacancy wake-up as in oxide ferroelectrics.

title: Printed magnetoelectric composite written by voltage, not current
idea: IFR: magnetic bits written with zero current. Closest achievable: print magnetostrictive CoFe2O4 nanoparticles in piezoelectric P(VDF-TrFE); a voltage strains the matrix and rotates particle magnetization between two easy axes, read by a printed magnetoresistive sensor line.
why: Nonvolatile, write energy is just the CV^2 of a printed capacitor (fact 10), unlimited magnetic endurance; R2R printable.

title: Printed vacuum nanogap access device with near-zero leakage
idea: IFR: the ideal insulator is nothing at all. Closest achievable: R2R-print electrodes and open ~10 nm nanogaps by controlled film cracking or sacrificial-layer removal, forming field-emission vacuum switches that conduct only above emission voltage, so a printed capacitor keeps its charge for hours.
why: Fact 3: leakage tail eliminated without needing a high-quality semiconductor; fully printable.

title: Open printed-memory PDK and ink library for distributed iteration
idea: IFR: thousands of labs test a new storage element every week at near-zero cost. Closest achievable: publish an open R2R process kit (standard printed electrode and access layers, test-structure layouts, characterization scripts) plus a shared ink bank so any lab can drop a new storage ink into a known stack.
why: Speeds discovery and grows the U.S. talent base; cost per experiment drops from ~$100k fab shuttle to ~$100 print run.

title: Printed spin-crossover film held inside its room-temperature hysteresis
idea: IFR: a molecule that remembers its spin state at no cost. Closest achievable: print [Fe(Htrz)2(trz)]-class nanoparticles with a ~40 K wide hysteresis loop, hold the array at mid-loop temperature, set high-spin with a ns local heat pulse and low-spin with a piezo strain pulse, and read the ~10% volume/dielectric change.
why: Nonvolatile within the operating window, molecular switching with no wear, all-printed; write energy is the risk.

title: MLCC-style tape-cast 3D capacitor stack for printed DRAM
idea: IFR: 3D DRAM capacitors made the way industry already prints trillions of MLCCs a year. Closest achievable: tape-cast and screen-print 0.5 um BaTiO3 layers (k~2000) with printed Ni electrodes into a 100-layer stack whose per-layer pads are addressed by printed oxide-TFT selectors on the stack edge; 1 um^2 at 0.5 um already gives ~35 fF.
why: Facts 1 and 2: 7x the needed charge without high AR; MLCC lines use no EUV and cost cents per part, so capital per bit drops by orders.

title: Printed molecular-rotor framework where dipolar guests store the bit
idea: IFR: a crystal of identical, frictionless dipole switches. Closest achievable: print a metal-organic framework film whose pores hold polar rotor molecules that align up or down under a field and stay pinned by tuned ~0.8 eV rotational barriers, read as polarization charge.
why: Facts 1 and 10: molecular-scale bit with low switching barrier, printed from MOF inks at low temperature; no defect migration so endurance is high.

title: Printed conducting-polymer ion-doping bit read as channel conductance
idea: IFR: a transistor whose channel is itself the memory. Closest achievable: an organic electrochemical transistor (PEDOT:PSS class) where a pulse pushes ions into or out of the printed channel and a barrier layer pins them; read current is nondestructive and multilevel.
why: Fact 8 and cost: nondestructive read on printed foil; small devices have reached sub-us switching, and 100 nm scaling targets tens of ns.

title: Printed charge-coupled shift-register memory with no per-bit transistor
idea: IFR: memory with zero transistors per bit. Closest achievable: print clocked electrode rows on a continuous oxide-semiconductor film so charge packets shift CCD-style along short lanes to a single sense node per lane; many short lanes keep latency near 100 ns.
why: Facts 7 and 4: removes per-cell access devices and most periphery; only printed electrodes needed, so capital and lithography collapse.

title: Electrophoretic nanoparticle bit shuttling across a printed nanocell
idea: IFR: e-paper bistability at DRAM speed. Closest achievable: confine one charged nanoparticle in a printed ~10 nm fluid cell; a field pulse drives it to either electrode (transit ~10 ns at 10 nm), van der Waals force holds it there, and the bit reads as a capacitance shift.
why: Zero retention power, no solid-state wear (unlimited endurance), printable fluid cells.

title: Printed metal-insulator-metal tunnel diode replaces access transistor
idea: IFR: an access device that is only a sandwich. Closest achievable: use a printed Ta2O5 or Al2O3 MIM diode, as in early active-matrix LCDs, as a two-terminal nonlinear access device for each printed storage capacitor; strong I-V nonlinearity isolates half-selected cells.
why: Facts 7 and 4: two-terminal printed access removes TFT gate layers, giving a printable 4F^2 crosspoint cell.

title: Printed relaxor terpolymer dielectric reaching k of 50
idea: IFR: a printable dielectric with ceramic-class permittivity. Closest achievable: slot-die coat P(VDF-TrFE-CFE) relaxor terpolymer (k ~50 at room temperature, slim hysteresis) as the storage-capacitor dielectric, optionally loaded with BaTiO3 nanocubes to push higher.
why: Fact 1: approaches the k~70 target in a printable low-temperature film at cents per area.

title: Roll-to-roll transferred monolayer MoS2 gain cell
idea: IFR: an access channel too thin to leak. Closest achievable: R2R-transfer CVD monolayer MoS2 (1.8-2 eV gap, 0.7 nm thick, ideal electrostatics) onto foil to build 2T0C gain cells where the read-transistor gate is the storage node, with off-currents below 1e-18 A.
why: Facts 3 and 2: refresh interval stretches to seconds; 2D films laminate layer by layer into printed 3D stacks.

title: Van der Waals adhesion-latched printed nanocantilever bit
idea: IFR: turn stiction, the classic MEMS failure, into the memory. Closest achievable: nanoimprint a cantilever over a printed electrode coated with an anti-wear monolayer; once pulled in, van der Waals adhesion holds it on until a reverse electrostatic or thermal pulse releases it.
why: Zero retention power and nonvolatile; printable via imprint plus sacrificial layer; contact endurance is the risk.

title: Memory wallpaper: square metres of printed foil DRAM
idea: IFR: memory as cheap per area as a solar panel. Closest achievable: print 1T1C oxide-TFT cells at 2 um pitch on PV-grade foil (~2.5e7 bits/cm^2, ~30 GB per m^2 at ~$50/m^2) and mount panels as a capacity tier behind HBM/DDR.
why: Cost per bit (~$2/GB) and capital (PV-class lines) at the price of us-class latency; adds supply outside DRAM fabs.

title: Self-rolling Swiss-roll nanomembrane capacitors printed flat
idea: IFR: a capacitor that folds itself into 3D. Closest achievable: print a strained bilayer carrying dielectric and electrode layers on a sacrificial film; releasing it makes the stack roll into a multi-turn tube, multiplying plate area 10-50x per footprint.
why: Fact 1: high Cs from planar printing, no high-AR etch and no EUV.

title: Retool idle U.S. thin-film PV and flexible-display lines as memory fabs
idea: IFR: memory capacity appears without building fabs. Closest achievable: buy or lease idle R2R thin-film PV and flexible OLED lines, add a printed storage-element module, and ship foil memory tiers within 12-18 months.
why: Capital and time (fact 4): line cost ~$100M vs $15B; raises U.S. manufacturability.
